question: Which long-term health problem is strongly linked to long-term Schistosoma haematobium infection?

options.A: Bladder cancer
options.B: Bone marrow depression
options.C: Lung failure
options.D: Gastric ulcers

explanation: Years of chronic irritation in the bladder from trapped eggs can unfortunately lead to cellular changes and bladder cancer. Another great reason why early treatment matters so much! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h7)

question: Long before modern labs, how did early humans figure out which foods were safe to eat?

options.A: Microscopic testing
options.B: Written government guidelines
options.C: Trial and error
options.D: Chemical analysis

explanation: Spot on! Before science labs, our ancestors had to rely on simple observation and trying things out to see what was safe to put in their bodies. [learn more](GNS227_U1_T002#GNS227_U1_T002_h1)

question: You receive your handoff report and hear about four different tasks. Which one needs your immediate action?

options.A: A non-urgent blood pressure check for a stable patient
options.B: A missing signature on a nursing admission form from yesterday
options.C: A patient reporting sudden chest pain and shortness of breath
options.D: A routine discharge education session scheduled for the afternoon

explanation: Spot on! Chest pain and trouble breathing point to an emergency that takes priority over any routine paperwork. [learn more](GST321_U6_T1#GST321_U6_T1_h6)

question: Why must nurses monitor mental status closely in a patient with advanced portal hypertension?

options.A: To evaluate how well oral pain medications are working
options.B: To catch early signs of hepatic encephalopathy caused by toxin buildup
options.C: To check if the patient is getting enough sleep at night
options.D: To determine if the patient is experiencing a sudden stroke

explanation: When blood bypasses the liver through detour vessels, toxins like ammonia aren't filtered out and reach the brain. Checking mental alertness helps us catch early signs of confusion (hepatic encephalopathy) right away! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h5)

question: Why do regular antibiotics like standard penicillin fail against tuberculosis?

options.A: Penicillin only works on viruses, and TB is a fungus
options.B: Human stomach acid destroys penicillin before it reaches the lungs
options.C: The waxy outer cell wall of TB blocks standard drugs from entering
options.D: Tuberculosis bacteria move too fast for penicillin to catch them

explanation: TB bacteria have a tough, waxy outer coat that standard antibiotics just can't break through. That's why special anti-TB drugs are a must! [learn more](GNS223_U2_T6#GNS223_U2_T6_h3)

question: How do airborne pathogens primarily travel to a new host?

options.A: Via large wet respiratory splashes falling straight to the floor
options.B: Through direct physical handshakes with infected individuals
options.C: By clinging to the legs of biting insects or household pets
options.D: As tiny dried droplet nuclei suspended in air currents

explanation: Airborne pathogens are so small and light that they float in the air for hours and travel long distances before being inhaled. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: What happens during biological magnification (biomagnification) in a food chain?

options.A: Microbiological pathogens are neutralized by natural river currents
options.B: Fish grow larger and healthier due to the presence of mineral nutrients
options.C: Algae populations decrease rapidly due to cold water temperatures
options.D: Toxic chemicals become more concentrated in predators at higher trophic levels

explanation: Correct! As small creatures eat toxins and get eaten by bigger fish and animals, the poison multiplies and gets stronger higher up the food chain. [learn more](GST114_U6_T6#GST114_U6_T6_h5)

question: Why do we test changes on a small scale using the PDSA cycle first?

options.A: To ensure that patients never notice when a new policy starts
options.B: To make sure the project takes as long as possible to complete
options.C: To hide mistakes from hospital management and senior nurses
options.D: To minimize risks and avoid wasting resources if the change fails

explanation: Exactly! Testing small lets us see if an idea actually works in real life before rolling it out to the whole ward, saving time and stress. [learn more](GST319_U3_T5#GST319_U3_T5_h2)

question: A manager watches a nurse perform a sterile dressing change to ensure correct technique. What type of control is this?

options.A: Feedforward control
options.B: Concurrent control
options.C: Financial control
options.D: Feedback control

explanation: Observing care as it happens lets the manager catch and fix mistakes on the spot. That's concurrent control! [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h3)

question: What is the main job of a vehicle when diluting a lotion?

options.A: To act as a safe base that mixes well with the active drug
options.B: To completely neutralize the active drug's healing properties
options.C: To add a strong fragrance to cover up chemical odors
options.D: To change a liquid medication into a hard tablet

explanation: Think of the vehicle as a friendly carrier base that helps you spread the active medicine evenly without fuss. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h3)

question: When designing public health education, what does 'acceptability' mean?

options.A: Whether the target community welcomes and relates to the educational tool
options.B: Whether the government health ministry has stamped it with an official seal
options.C: How many pages of text the target population is willing to read
options.D: How cheaply the printing press can manufacture the paper flyers

explanation: Acceptability is all about whether the community feels comfortable with the material and feels it matches their personal values and beliefs. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T6#GNS124_U5_T6_h2)

question: Which breathing sign is a classic warning of severe respiratory distress in a newborn?

options.A: Regular periodic breathing
options.B: Expiratory grunting
options.C: Deep abdominal snoring
options.D: Slow, quiet inspirations

explanation: When a baby makes a grunting sound as they breathe out, it's their way of trying to keep their tiny air sacs (alveoli) open. It's a red flag that they are struggling to breathe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h6)

question: How many daily medications do doctors usually mean when they talk about polypharmacy?

options.A: Taking two or more medications daily
options.B: Taking ten or more medications daily
options.C: Taking only herbal remedies alongside drugs
options.D: Taking five or more medications daily

explanation: You'll often hear this in the ward! Polypharmacy simply means a patient is taking five or more regular medications at the same time. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why is high blood pressure often called a 'silent killer'?

options.A: It stops the heart completely without warning signs.
options.B: It causes sudden deafness before any physical pain starts.
options.C: It rarely produces early symptoms until serious organ damage occurs.
options.D: It only strikes individuals while they are fast asleep at night.

explanation: You got it! High blood pressure can quietly damage the body for years without any warning signs, which is why regular checks are so important. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h1)

question: Where in the digestive tract do most oral drugs actually get absorbed into the body?

options.A: The small intestine
options.B: The esophagus
options.C: The stomach
options.D: The large intestine

explanation: The small intestine is the champion of absorption! With its massive surface area covered in tiny villi, it's the main highway for drugs to enter the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T4#GNS125_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is another name for the Pouch of Douglas in female anatomy?

options.A: Rectouterine pouch
options.B: Broad ligament recess
options.C: Vesicouterine pouch
options.D: Parametrial space

explanation: You've got this! We call it the rectouterine pouch because it sits right between the rectum and the uterus. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T27#GNS216_U5_T27_h1)

question: What is the primary role of nutrition in clinical nursing care?

options.A: Lowering hospital cleaning costs
options.B: Replacing the need for routine medications
options.C: Accelerating nursing shift handovers
options.D: Serving as a therapeutic tool for healing

explanation: Food and proper nutrition provide the essential building blocks the body needs to repair tissues and fight off disease, making it a key part of medical treatment. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T001#GNS227_U2_T001_h1)

question: Why should a nurse keep sentences short and clear when speaking to a disaster survivor?

options.A: Survivors usually have poor hearing after a disaster
options.B: Trauma and shock impair concentration and memory
options.C: Long sentences cost too much valuable time
options.D: Hospital regulations require brief communication

explanation: High stress levels make it difficult for survivors to process complex information or long explanations. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T6#GNS315_U5_T6_h7)

question: What is the main goal of using the 'Cluster Approach' in international disaster management?

options.A: To allow military forces to take full command of civilian healthcare facilities
options.B: To group humanitarian organizations by sector to improve coordination and accountability
options.C: To centralize all international financial donations into one bank account
options.D: To ensure that every NGO operates independently without government oversight

explanation: Brilliant! The cluster system groups agencies by their specialty (like health or water) so everyone works together cleanly without overlapping or missing needs. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T10#GNS315_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the main goal of contact tracing during an infectious disease outbreak?

options.A: To find out which hospital ward cost the most money
options.B: To collect financial donations from family members
options.C: To monitor exposed individuals and catch new cases early
options.D: To test new pharmaceutical drugs on healthy volunteers

explanation: Well done! Tracking down people who were exposed lets us watch them closely and isolate them before they can spread the illness further. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: Which type of exercise involves the nurse moving the joints of a patient who cannot move at all?

options.A: Passive exercises
options.B: Resistive exercises
options.C: Active exercises
options.D: Active-assistive exercises

explanation: When a patient cannot move their limbs themselves, you step in and gently move their joints for them. That is what passive exercises are all about! [learn more](GNS221_U1_T4#GNS221_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is a nurse's legal duty when it comes to suspected child abuse?

options.A: Mediator between parents and social welfare agencies
options.B: Mandated reporter required by law to report suspicions
options.C: Private counselor exempt from state reporting rules
options.D: Neutral observer who must first confirm absolute proof

explanation: As a nurse, you are legally required to speak up and report any reasonable suspicion to keep the child safe. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T24#GNS225_U5_T24_h6)

question: What is the core idea behind deductive reasoning?

options.A: Trusting a senior doctor purely because of their title
options.B: Moving from a general premise down to a specific conclusion
options.C: Accepting traditional habits without asking any questions
options.D: Gathering random facts until a pattern appears by chance

explanation: Deduction takes a known general rule and applies it to a specific situation to figure out what follows. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which of the following describes affective conflict?

options.A: An emotional clash driven by personality differences
options.B: A healthy debate over a new hospital protocol
options.C: A disagreement about medication dosages
options.D: A structural fight over ward budgets

explanation: Affective conflict involves feelings, ego, and interpersonal animosity rather than professional tasks. [learn more](GST321_U5_T3#GST321_U5_T3_h6)

question: How do positive reinforcement and validation from significant others affect a teenager?

options.A: They cause long-term dependency on medical providers.
options.B: They trigger frequent behavioral outbursts in public.
options.C: They lower academic performance due to overconfidence.
options.D: They build emotional resilience and healthy self-esteem.

explanation: Supportive relationships foster psychological safety, helping teenagers develop strong coping skills and healthy self-regard. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T20#GNS312_U3_T20_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of documentation in palliative care?

options.A: To ensure clear communication of care goals across different disciplines
options.B: To prove to insurance companies that treatments are expensive
options.C: To replace verbal communication between nursing shifts completely
options.D: To protect the hospital legally from patient lawsuits

explanation: Good records ensure that every doctor, nurse, and therapist on the team knows the current plan and the patient's wishes. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T4#GNS321_U4_T4_h9)

question: In community health nursing, who is considered your primary client?

options.A: Only the head of the household
options.B: Private paying clients in clinics
options.C: Patients admitted to the surgical ward
options.D: The entire community or population

explanation: Exactly! The heart of public health nursing is treating the whole community—not just one person—as your main patient. [learn more](GNS225_U1_T8#GNS225_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to chat about a patient's daily routine before choosing a birth control method?

options.A: To match the patient with a method they can use consistently
options.B: To test the patient's ability to read complex medical textbooks
options.C: To calculate the exact financial tax for purchasing the drugs
options.D: To determine if the patient has any hidden genetic disorders

explanation: Great nursing care is personalized! Knowing a patient's lifestyle helps you suggest a method—like a daily pill versus a 3-year implant—that genuinely fits their everyday life. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h8)

question: Why are sympathetic preganglionic fibers usually shorter than the postganglionic fibers?

options.A: Because target organs are located directly next to the brain
options.B: Because they must travel long distances inside the spinal canal
options.C: Because they release hormones directly into the bloodstream
options.D: Because sympathetic ganglia sit close to the spinal cord

explanation: The relay stations (ganglia) hang out right next to the spinal cord in a chain. This means a short first hop (preganglionic) and a longer second hop (postganglionic) to reach the organs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T30#GNS211_U3_T30_h2)

question: Why do older adults often react much more strongly to standard drug doses than younger people?

options.A: The stomach absorbs medications completely without any filtration.
options.B: Brain cells multiply rapidly, increasing chemical reactions.
options.C: Kidney and liver function naturally decline with age, slowing drug clearance.
options.D: Older adults digest all food and medicine much faster than young adults.

explanation: Great thinking! Because the kidneys and liver process things a bit more slowly as we age, medicines stay in the body longer, increasing the risk of side effects. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T1#GNS324_U3_T1_h5)

question: What makes adaptive immunity so special compared to innate immunity?

options.A: It relies entirely on physical barriers like unbroken skin layers
options.B: It responds instantly within the first few minutes of exposure
options.C: It creates specific immunological memory against specific pathogens
options.D: It requires no cellular coordination or chemical signaling

explanation: Spot on! Adaptive immunity never forgets. Once it fights a germ, it remembers it, so if that same germ attacks later, your body fights back much faster and stronger. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why is natural daylight or color-corrected light best when checking a patient's skin?

options.A: It eliminates the need to wear protective examination gloves
options.B: It magnifies tiny skin lesions without needing specialized glass tools
options.C: It prevents misinterpreting subtle color changes like jaundice or cyanosis
options.D: It ensures the patient stays warm during a full physical examination

explanation: Yellow room lights can trick your eyes, making it hard to spot important color changes like yellow skin (jaundice) or a bluish tint (cyanosis). [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does drug tolerance mean?

options.A: Having an allergic skin rash develop after starting a new prescription
options.B: The body clearing the medication from the kidneys within minutes
options.C: Experiencing severe tremors immediately after taking a single pill
options.D: Needing larger doses of a drug over time to get the same physical effect

explanation: Tolerance happens when the body gets so used to a drug that it takes a higher dose to feel the same result. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h6)

question: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), how is health best defined today?

options.A: Having adequate financial resources to access medication
options.B: The total absence of diagnosed chronic or acute illnesses
options.C: A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being
options.D: Living in a rural area with low population density

explanation: You've got this! Modern health isn't just about not being sick in bed—it looks at your whole life: physical, mental, and social wellness combined. [learn more](GNS225_U1_T5#GNS225_U1_T5_h1)

question: What type of care usually triggers automatic DRF exemptions during an emergency?

options.A: Long-term physical therapy
options.B: Annual medical fitness checkups
options.C: Emergency trauma resuscitation
options.D: Routine elective cosmetic surgery

explanation: When every second counts, emergency trauma care gets fast-tracked so lifesaving supplies are never delayed by paperwork. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T6#GNS215_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why is keeping track of information so important for UNOCHA during a major disaster?

options.A: It prevents duplication of relief efforts and identifies gaps in aid delivery
options.B: It replaces the need for local health assessments by foreign doctors
options.C: It allows the agency to control all financial transactions in the host country
options.D: It guarantees that political leaders will fund the recovery process

explanation: Exactly! By tracking who is doing what, we make sure food and medicine reach every community without wasting supplies or leaving anyone out. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T10#GNS315_U1_T10_h2)

question: A nurse uses the hospital computer to check the medical chart of a famous musician admitted to a different ward, simply out of personal curiosity. What is the legal and ethical status of this action?

options.A: It is allowed if the nurse is off-duty during the chart review
options.B: It is acceptable as long as the nurse does not tell anyone else
options.C: It is a serious privacy breach because the nurse is outside the circle of care
options.D: It is encouraged so staff can offer collective words of encouragement

explanation: Looking at charts without a direct professional need for patient care violates data privacy laws and ethics. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T4#GNS113_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why do viral infections usually NOT produce thick pus the way bacterial infections do?

options.A: Viruses live strictly on the outer surface of the skin where pus cannot form.
options.B: Viruses only infect red blood cells, which lack the ability to cause inflammation.
options.C: Viruses instantly destroy all white blood cells in the human body on contact.
options.D: Viruses do not recruit large numbers of pus-forming neutrophils in the same way pyogenic bacteria do.

explanation: Pus is mostly packed with neutrophils responding to bacteria. Viruses trigger a different immune response, so you don't get that classic thick pus. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why must an occupational health nurse team up with safety officers and management?

options.A: To manage the daily production schedule of the factory floor
options.B: To audit financial records for the company's medical insurance
options.C: To handle legal lawsuits filed against injured employees
options.D: To ensure working conditions meet acceptable health standards

explanation: You got it! Working hand-in-hand with safety teams helps the nurse keep the work environment safe and healthy for everyone. [learn more](GNS225_U7_T3#GNS225_U7_T3_h1)

question: What is the medical term when a patient is taking multiple medications all at once?

options.A: Polypharmacy
options.B: Anaphylaxis
options.C: Idiosyncrasy
options.D: Pharmacovigilance

explanation: Poly means many, and pharmacy means drugs! Juggling many drugs at once increases the risk of side effects, but you've got this concept down. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the main role of regulatory bodies like NAFDAC in ensuring drug safety?

options.A: Prescribing standardized medications directly to patients in hospital wards
options.B: Manufacturing cheap synthetic substitutes for expensive imported drugs
options.C: Inspecting manufacturing plants and testing drug batches for purity and accurate dosage
options.D: Growing raw medicinal plants in government-owned botanical gardens

explanation: NAFDAC protects our health by checking factories, testing drug purity, and making sure medications are safe before they reach patients. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T3#GNS125_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which of these signs is the classic giveaway that an IV has 'infiltrated' (leaked into the tissue)?

options.A: A warm, red, hard streak running all the way up the arm
options.B: Severe chest pain accompanied by audible lung crackles
options.C: Bright red bleeding gushing out around the plastic catheter
options.D: Swelling, coolness, and pallor around the insertion site

explanation: Spot on! When IV fluid leaks into the tissue instead of the vein, it makes the skin look pale, feel cool, and swell up. Time to restart the line! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: A nurse assesses a wound and notes it as 'mild, moderate, or severe'. What scale of measurement is this?

options.A: Ratio scale
options.B: Nominal scale
options.C: Interval scale
options.D: Ordinal scale

explanation: Because the wound grades follow a clear rank order from best to worst, we call this an ordinal scale. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T1#GNS217_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why should loose throw rugs be removed from a patient's home after surgery?

options.A: They easily slide underfoot and cause dangerous falls.
options.B: They prevent the wheelchair wheels from rolling smoothly.
options.C: They trap moisture and cause the home humidity to rise.
options.D: They block the medical equipment from plugging into the wall.

explanation: Unsecured rugs love to slip on smooth floors, making them a major tripping hazard for anyone learning to get around with new supports. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h8)

question: A patient with unsteady balance prepares for discharge home. What is the best nursing action to address home safety?

options.A: Discuss removing tripping hazards and installing bathroom grab bars
options.B: Advise the patient to remain in bed until fully recovered
options.C: Recommend replacing all furniture with hospital-grade equipment
options.D: Suggest wearing thick socks for warmth and comfort while walking

explanation: Practical modifications like clearing walkways and adding bathroom grab bars directly prevent falls in the living environment. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is participatory management in nursing administration?

options.A: Allowing patients to write their own medication prescriptions
options.B: Leaving all hospital decisions entirely to government ministers
options.C: Involving staff nurses in decision-making processes like shift planning
options.D: Banning staff meetings to save time during busy shifts

explanation: Participatory management means management doesn't just bark orders; they bring nurses into the conversation when making decisions that affect the ward. [learn more](GST321_U2_T2#GST321_U2_T2_h7)

question: What is the everyday medical name for the outer, visible part of the ear?

options.A: Eustachian tube
options.B: Tympanic membrane
options.C: Auricle
options.D: Cochlea

explanation: Great job! The auricle (or pinna) is shaped just right to catch sounds and funnel them down into the ear canal. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T2#GNS211_U4_T2_h2)

question: Why must nurses keep a close eye on blood sugar levels for patients on high-dose IV steroids, even if they don't have diabetes?

options.A: Steroids destroy pancreatic beta cells within the first few hours
options.B: Steroids cause severe dehydration that artificially concentrates sugar
options.C: Steroids increase the patient's appetite for high-sugar foods
options.D: Steroids stimulate glucose production and impair insulin utilization

explanation: Steroids encourage the liver to release more glucose while making body cells temporarily ignore insulin. This combo naturally causes blood sugar to rise! [learn more](GNS223_U7_T4#GNS223_U7_T4_h5)

question: Why are sugary carbonated drinks a poor choice for everyday hydration in teens?

options.A: They contain too much pure protein for growing kidneys.
options.B: They instantly cause permanent tooth decay on first contact.
options.C: They lower body temperature to dangerous levels.
options.D: They cause blood sugar spikes and do not hydrate efficiently.

explanation: Too much sugar slows down how fast the stomach empties liquids, meaning sugary drinks don't quench thirst or hydrate as well as plain water. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T007#GNS227_U2_T007_h4)

question: According to the Swiss Cheese Model, when does a critical incident or accident actually happen?

options.A: When holes in all defense layers align at the same time
options.B: When the hospital management changes all safety policies
options.C: When a single nurse makes a minor math calculation error
options.D: When a patient refuses to take prescribed medications

explanation: Brilliant! Accidents happen only when multiple safety barriers fail simultaneously, letting the error reach the patient. Keep pushing forward! [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h2)

question: Why do we need clear referral pathways from community clinics up to Tier 4 specialists?

options.A: To replace basic physical healthcare with hospital admission
options.B: So that every single citizen in the community ends up seeing a psychiatrist
options.C: To ensure that patients with severe psychiatric conditions reach qualified specialists promptly
options.D: To prevent community volunteers from ever talking to distressed families

explanation: Smooth referrals make sure that patients slipping past basic care are quickly connected to the experts who can help them best. [learn more](GNS314_U6_T5#GNS314_U6_T5_h5)

question: In patient safety terminology, who is considered the 'second victim' of a medical error?

options.A: The hospital administrator who has to pay for the resulting legal settlement
options.B: The pharmacist who dispensed the medication two shifts prior
options.C: The family member who was visiting the patient at the time of the event
options.D: The healthcare provider involved in the incident who experiences emotional trauma

explanation: The second victim refers to clinicians who experience profound emotional distress and guilt after being involved in an adverse event. [learn more](GST319_U6_T1#GST319_U6_T1_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of regular team conferences in home health care?

options.A: To review patient progress and update the unified care plan
options.B: To reduce the number of home visits required by the agency
options.C: To replace written medical documentation in patient charts
options.D: To evaluate the personal performance of the nursing staff

explanation: Team conferences bring professionals together to share updates, evaluate goals, and adjust care strategies based on current needs. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T4#GNS324_U1_T4_h6)

question: What advice should you give a patient about sex while she is undergoing treatment for an infection?

options.A: Increase sexual frequency to help flush out the remaining bacteria
options.B: Stop sexual activity only for the first two hours after taking drugs
options.C: Abstain from sexual intercourse until treatment is finished and cure is confirmed
options.D: Continue normal sexual activity as long as condoms are used

explanation: Advise her to pause sexual activity until she finishes her meds and gets the all-clear. This stops reinfection and gives her body time to heal. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T4#GNS216_U5_T4_h7)

question: What is the best way for a community health nurse to handle local rumors about vaccine safety?

options.A: Engage community leaders in open dialogue and health education
options.B: Ignore the community complaints and focus only on paperwork
options.C: Scold parents who ask questions about vaccine ingredients
options.D: Close down the immunization clinic until rumors stop spreading

explanation: Teaming up with trusted community leaders and providing respectful, clear health talks is the best way to clear up fears and build trust. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T75#GNS214_U1_T75_h7)

question: Why is it usually a bad idea to use a young child or relative as an interpreter for complex medication instructions?

options.A: Using family members violates hospital financial accounting protocols
options.B: Family members may unintentionally omit or misinterpret complex medical details
options.C: Family members are legally barred from knowing medication dosages
options.D: Relative interpreters always make the patient feel more anxious than strangers

explanation: Loved ones want to help, but medical terms are tricky. They might miss vital dosage warnings by accident, so a trained interpreter is always safer. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T6#GNS215_U4_T6_h3)

question: A nursing mother is three weeks postpartum and resting in bed. Why is she still at risk for a blood clot (deep vein thrombosis)?

options.A: Her white blood cell count remains elevated due to breastfeeding
options.B: Her plasma volume expands even further during the fourth week
options.C: Her red blood cell count instantly drops to zero after childbirth
options.D: The hypercoagulable state of pregnancy lingers for several weeks

explanation: Even after birth, the body's clotting system takes a few weeks to settle back to normal, which is why we must keep a close eye on new mums. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T1#GNS121_U7_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of nursing research?

options.A: To increase the cost of hospital equipment
options.B: To replace clinical judgment with rigid rules
options.C: To give doctors more administrative duties
options.D: To expand knowledge and improve patient care

explanation: Research is fundamentally about discovering new information that directly enhances how nurses care for their patients. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which part of a plant is most commonly used in traditional remedies?

options.A: Taproot only
options.B: Pollen grains
options.C: Leaves
options.D: Heartwood

question: What are the main parts of Post-Abortion Care (PAC)?

question: Why do educators evaluate a learning activity after you've completed it?

question: Why must Nigerian nurses understand local health-seeking behaviors?

question: What makes primary health care nurses so crucial for disease surveillance?

question: What does the term 'fidelity' mean when talking about healthcare simulators?

question: At what point should healthcare waste be sorted or segregated?

question: During a massive disaster with limited supplies, how should medical items be shared out?

question: Why is it important for a nurse manager to understand their hospital's chain of command?

question: How do school health programs help keep female students in class?

question: A patient gets a wound infection after a nurse uses an uncleaned blood pressure cuff. What kind of spread is this?

question: What is the main focus of qualitative research in healthcare?

question: Why are schools considered ideal settings for health promotion?

question: You are preparing a postpartum mother with severe bleeding for emergency transfer. What is an essential step?

question: A patient insists on an IV infusion at a private pharmacy because they paid cash and want visible treatment. What factor is primarily at play here?

question: What happens to the thymus gland as a person grows older?

question: When you connect a struggling family with local social welfare resources and community support groups, what role are you performing?

question: What is the main focus of primordial prevention?

question: What is the term for the outcome that a nurse researcher measures in an experiment?

question: Why is it important to use local languages and traditional communication channels for immunization campaigns?

question: What is the primary focus of pharmacovigilance?

question: What does medication adherence mean in nursing care?

question: Which common lab test is used to screen patients for anemia?

question: Which of the following is a major environmental barrier to effective health communication in a clinic?

question: A patient arrives at a local primary health clinic with a deep, bleeding wound and signs of shock. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

question: Why is observation often more reliable than interviews in research?

question: What is the main goal of routine GI screenings like a colonoscopy?

question: Which physical sign do patients very often report when they are feeling extremely anxious?

question: What do we call the social, economic, and environmental factors that shape people's health?

question: Why are children under five especially vulnerable during a community disaster?

question: What is one of the most important roles of a nurse in a pediatric care team?

question: A patient has a red, swollen, tender gluteal injection site. What extra sign would tell you the sciatic nerve might be involved?

question: A nurse notices dried blood on a clamp coming out of the washer. What should be done?

question: What is the purpose of an EMR audit trail?

question: Which group of workers faces the highest daily risk of exposure to bloodborne infections like HIV and Hepatitis B?

question: What should day care staff do when they notice a child showing signs of a developmental delay?

question: Who is considered a vital stakeholder in a nursing quality improvement project?

question: Why are 4th-generation HIV tests that check for p24 antigens so helpful for early diagnosis?

question: What is a common complication when anxiety disorders are left untreated for many years?

options.B: To ensure the hospital saves money on meals
options.C: To follow strict government nursing regulations
options.D: To prove that traditional beliefs are always scientifically correct

explanation: When we respect our patients' beliefs instead of judging them, they feel safe and are more likely to share their real health habits with us. Great nursing is all about connection! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h1)

question: A client wants a specific pill, but it is unsafe for her because she has severe high blood pressure. What should you do first?

options.A: Give her the requested pill anyway to make her happy
options.B: Send her straight to a big teaching hospital for surgery
options.C: Scold her for choosing a bad medication without asking
options.D: Explain the health risk gently and discuss safer options

explanation: You got it! Patient safety comes first. We calmly explain why a drug isn't safe and gladly help them pick a better alternative. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h4)

question: Why is cultural humility important when providing dietary advice?

options.A: All cultures eat the exact same foods anyway
options.B: Food carries deep emotional and cultural meaning for patients
options.C: Patients will report the nurse to the police if local dishes are ignored
options.D: It proves to the doctor that the nurse is well-traveled

explanation: Respecting cultural food practices ensures the patient feels valued and is more likely to engage in constructive health talks. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T001#GNS227_U7_T001_h6)

question: Why do inactivated (killed) vaccines often need multiple booster doses?

options.A: The live virus inside them multiplies too quickly
options.B: The killed organisms produce a weaker immune response than live ones
options.C: They do not contain any antigens to trigger B-cells
options.D: They destroy existing memory cells in the bloodstream

explanation: You nailed it! Since the germs are dead and can't multiply, boosters give our immune system a helpful reminder to keep us protected. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h3)

question: Your patient knows how to inject their own insulin, but they need you to teach them how to calculate food portions. Which of Orem's systems is this?

options.A: Environmental control system
options.B: Supportive-educative system
options.C: Partially compensatory system
options.D: Fully compensatory system

explanation: Well done! In a supportive-educative system, the patient can do most things themselves, but they still need guidance, teaching, and support from you. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T6#GNS112_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary function of vitamins and minerals in our metabolism?

options.A: Acting as cofactors and coenzymes to support biochemical reactions
options.B: Providing the majority of daily calories for intense physical work
options.C: Storing extra energy in fat cells beneath the skin
options.D: Acting as the main structural framework for bone density

explanation: Well done! Think of vitamins and minerals as the helpful spark plugs that allow your body's cellular machinery to run smoothly. [learn more](GNS227_U1_T013#GNS227_U1_T013_h4)

question: Which sign should immediately make a nurse suspect a post-procedure perforation after an esophageal dilation?

options.A: A slight drop in blood pressure after resting
options.B: Sudden severe chest pain and rising heart rate
options.C: Mild sore throat when swallowing saliva
options.D: Low-grade nausea from mild residual sedation

explanation: If a patient suddenly gets severe, worsening chest pain and a fast heart rate (tachycardia), it's a huge red flag that there might be a tear leaking into the chest cavity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: How does losing access to school affect a young bride's future?

options.A: It makes her physically unable to speak clearly to healthcare workers
options.B: It limits her ability to earn money and understand basic health information
options.C: It forces her to move permanently to a foreign country
options.D: It guarantees she will develop severe bone disorders in old age

explanation: Well reasoned! Without education, she misses out on financial independence and health awareness, keeping her trapped in vulnerability. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T13#GNS312_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why is it so important to leave enough space between tents when setting up a temporary disaster camp?

options.A: It helps prevent the rapid spread of airborne and contact illnesses
options.B: It ensures everyone gets the exact same size tent
options.C: It makes the camp look more organized for visitors
options.D: It allows heavy machinery to drive through the tents at night

explanation: When people are packed too tightly together, illnesses like coughs and infections spread like wildfire. Space keeps everyone safer! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h3)

question: What is the key difference between Acute Stress Disorder and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder?

options.A: Whether the patient has physical injuries or not
options.B: The time frame and duration of the symptoms
options.C: The age of the person experiencing the trauma
options.D: The specific type of disaster that caused the trauma

explanation: Acute Stress Disorder happens shortly after the event, whereas PTSD involves long-lasting symptoms that persist over months or years. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T6#GNS315_U5_T6_h3)

question: What is inter-sectorial collaboration in disaster management?

options.A: The independent operation of government ministries without outside help
options.B: The complete takeover of local clinics by the military during crises
options.C: The coordinated pooling of skills and resources by different agencies
options.D: The exclusive funding of emergency hospitals by private businesses

explanation: Think of it like group work in class—different agencies team up and share what they have to handle emergencies smoothly! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T8#GNS315_U5_T8_h1)

question: Which part of the nerve cell is mainly destroyed during the demyelination process in disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Gray matter neurons
options.C: Myelin sheath
options.D: Acetylcholine

explanation: You've got this! The immune system mistakenly attacks and strips away the myelin sheath, which normally acts like an insulation cover to protect nerves and speed up signals. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the main difference between statistical significance and clinical significance in nursing?

options.A: Statistical means the math is real, while clinical means it actually helps the patient
options.B: There is no difference; both terms mean exactly the same thing in healthcare
options.C: Clinical significance only matters in laboratories, whereas statistical matters at the bedside
options.D: Statistical significance is based on patient interviews, while clinical uses computers

explanation: You nailed it! Something can be proven by math (statistically significant), but still make barely any noticeable difference to an actual patient in the ward. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T15#GNS217_U4_T15_h6)

question: What happens when a researcher makes a Type I error?

options.A: Concluding a treatment works when it actually does not
options.B: Failing to notice that a treatment works when it actually does
options.C: Selecting a sample that is too small to represent the ward
options.D: Calculating the wrong average for patient blood pressures

explanation: Correct! A Type I error is like celebrating a false positive—thinking your new nursing routine helps patients when it really doesn't do anything special. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T3#GNS217_U4_T3_h5)

question: By about what percentage does plasma volume increase during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: 10 percent
options.B: 50 percent
options.C: 5 percent
options.D: 100 percent

explanation: Amazing! By the third trimester, a pregnant woman's plasma volume shoots up by nearly 50% to nourish the baby and placenta. The female body is truly incredible! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h2)

question: Why is chemoprophylaxis sometimes prescribed to health workers or travelers entering high-risk areas?

options.A: To eliminate the need for using protective clothing
options.B: To boost their red blood cell count against severe anemia
options.C: To permanently cure them of any genetic illnesses they carry
options.D: To prevent an infection from establishing itself if exposure happens

explanation: Chemoprophylaxis uses preventative medications to stop pathogens from multiplying inside the body following inevitable exposure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T7#GNS313_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why does the idea of 'agency' matter when you are carrying out your daily nursing duties?

options.A: It allows the nurse to change hospital policies without approval.
options.B: It means the nurse is personally exempt from all criminal laws.
options.C: It binds the hospital principal for acts done within employment scope.
options.D: It transfers complete medical licensing rights to the institution.

explanation: As a nurse acting within your normal duties, you represent the hospital. That means your professional actions on the job legally involve the hospital as your principal. Simple and clear! [learn more](GST321_U10_T4#GST321_U10_T4_h1)

question: Why must you remove a medication patch from a patient's chest before putting on AED pads?

options.A: The medication will instantly enter the machine and break the processor.
options.B: The patch makes the skin too slippery for the rescuer to press hard.
options.C: The patch will absorb the conductive gel and ruin the AED pads.
options.D: The patch can block the electrical current and cause skin burns.

explanation: Medication patches can interfere with the electricity and even cause nasty skin burns. Always peel them off and wipe the skin clean first! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h5)

question: Your instructor wants to grade how well you show empathy and active listening during a patient chat. Which tool is best suited for this?

options.A: A binary checklist of yes or no procedural steps
options.B: A rating scale with descriptive performance levels
options.C: A multiple-choice pharmacology quiz
options.D: A timed medication calculation test

explanation: Communication has shades of quality, so a rating scale works much better than a simple yes/no checkbox to capture how well you connect with patients. [learn more](GST321_U9_T3#GST321_U9_T3_h6)

question: What exactly is an adverse event in healthcare?

options.A: A patient refusing to take prescribed medication
options.B: A natural progression of a terminal disease
options.C: A normal side effect expected from surgery
options.D: An unintended injury caused by medical care

explanation: You've got this! An adverse event is simply unexpected harm that happens because of medical treatment, not from the disease itself. [learn more](GST319_U6_T2#GST319_U6_T2_h1)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading in home care?

options.A: Spraying household furniture with industrial bleach daily
options.B: Keeping all windows tightly closed during visits
options.C: Performing proper and frequent hand hygiene
options.D: Wearing sterile surgical gowns for every home visit

explanation: Good old handwashing and using alcohol rubs remove germs fast, protecting both you and your patient from cross-contamination. [learn more](GNS324_U2_T8#GNS324_U2_T8_h5)

question: What crucial safety rule must be kept in mind when treating a patient infected with Taenia solium?

options.A: Giving the medication exclusively through an intravenous infusion
options.B: Ensuring the patient fasts completely for one week prior to dosing
options.C: Preventing the patient from swallowing shed eggs to avoid cysticercosis
options.D: Keeping the patient isolated in a negative pressure room

explanation: Brilliant! If the patient vomits or has poor hygiene during treatment, they might accidentally swallow T. solium eggs and develop dangerous tissue cysts. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T24#GNS313_U2_T24_h6)

question: What is the main cause of neonatal tetanus in newborn babies?

options.A: Mother-to-child transmission across the placenta during birth
options.B: Unhygienic practices during umbilical cord cutting and care
options.C: Inhalation of airborne bacterial droplets from coughing adults
options.D: Consuming unpasteurized milk during the first week of life

explanation: Correct! Neonatal tetanus happens when tetanus germs get into the unhealed umbilical stump, often due to unsterilized instruments. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h4)

question: When working in community health, what does the helpful acronym 'IEC' stand for?

options.A: Infection, Environment, and Control
options.B: Information, Education, and Communication
options.C: Immunization, Evaluation, and Care
options.D: Investigation, Education, and Counseling

explanation: IEC stands for Information, Education, and Communication. You'll use these three core strategies every day to promote health and prevent disease in your communities! [learn more](GNS124_U5_T5#GNS124_U5_T5_h1)

question: How often should a client receive a DMPA (Depo-Provera) injection for birth control?

options.A: Every 6 months
options.B: Every 1 month
options.C: Every 3 months
options.D: Every 2 months

explanation: You've got this! DMPA gives steady hormonal protection when given once every 3 months (about 13 weeks). [learn more](GNS226_U6_T013#GNS226_U6_T013_h1)

question: Why is it important for different agencies to clearly know their roles during an emergency?

options.A: It guarantees that nurses receive higher hazard allowances than police officers
options.B: It prevents teams from stepping on each other's toes and wasting efforts
options.C: It ensures that only doctors are allowed to distribute relief materials
options.D: It allows private companies to bypass government health regulations safely

explanation: When everyone knows their specific job, rescue work runs fast and smoothly without doing the same task twice. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T8#GNS315_U5_T8_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of vocational training programs for persons with physical disabilities?

options.A: To train people exclusively for nursing careers
options.B: To provide practical skills for self-reliance and employment
options.C: To keep individuals occupied during long hospital stays
options.D: To replace formal university education entirely

explanation: Vocational training equips individuals with marketable skills so they can earn a living and achieve financial independence. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T16#GNS225_U5_T16_h4)

question: A community nurse notices that three children from the same household missed their measles vaccines. Which record system helped reveal this?

options.A: Monthly financial summary
options.B: Family folder
options.C: Staff attendance register
options.D: National drug ledger

explanation: Wonderful! Because family folders group household members together, it's easy for nurses to spot patterns and catch missed vaccines across siblings. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T13#GNS225_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the main problem in the heart during congestive heart failure?

options.A: The lungs stop producing oxygen for the bloodstream
options.B: The heart rate drops too low to circulate oxygen
options.C: The heart cannot pump blood efficiently to meet body demands
options.D: The valves close too tightly to allow blood flow

explanation: You've got this! Heart failure simply means the heart muscle is too tired or stiff to pump enough blood forward, leading to fluid backup. It's a common condition you'll see often on the wards. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T1#GNS223_U1_T1_h1)

question: On a busy hospital ward, what is the main reason we manage our time well as nurses?

options.A: Ensuring patient safety and clinical effectiveness
options.B: Completing every shift exactly thirty minutes early
options.C: Reducing the total number of assigned patients
options.D: Eliminating the need for patient documentation

explanation: You've got this! Time management isn't just about rushing through chores—it's about organizing care so our patients stay safe and get better results. [learn more](GST321_U4_T4#GST321_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why do doctors sometimes prescribe a short-term anti-inflammatory drug right when a patient starts taking a new uric acid-lowering medication?

options.A: To permanently cure high blood pressure and chronic kidney disease
options.B: To prevent new uric acid-lowering drugs from triggering a sudden flare-up
options.C: To speed up the digestion of purines in the stomach
options.D: To completely replace the need for drinking water every day

explanation: You're doing great! When uric acid drops, old crystals start breaking down and shifting around. This sudden movement can trick the body into a flare, so extra protection is given at the start. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T16#GNS222_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why do we use air ambulances for patients in remote areas?

options.A: It bridges the gap to advanced medical facilities
options.B: It is always cheaper than ground ambulance transport
options.C: Patients prefer flying over riding in cars
options.D: Hospitals do not accept ground transfers

explanation: Spot on! When patients are far away from big hospitals, air transport moves them quickly so they can get the high-level care they desperately need. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T14#GNS321_U2_T14_h1)

question: Why is patient coercion a serious worry during research recruitment?

options.A: Ethical boards do not allow patients to receive free medication
options.B: Coerced patients always give false answers on questionnaires
options.C: Patients might feel forced to join because their nurse or doctor asked
options.D: Hospital management requires a 100 percent recruitment rate

explanation: Brilliant! Patients respect their nurses and doctors so much that they might fear getting bad care if they say 'no,' which makes true voluntary consent tricky. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h7)

question: How does assisted living differ fundamentally from traditional skilled nursing homes?

options.A: It provides a homelike environment that emphasizes autonomy and help with daily tasks rather than heavy medical care
options.B: It relies entirely on family members to provide all professional nursing services
options.C: It refuses admission to any older adult who has a chronic medical condition
options.D: It operates strictly as a hospital ward for patients requiring mechanical ventilation

explanation: Assisted living is meant for folks who just need a little boost with daily activities (like bathing or dressing) but don't need round-the-clock intensive medical nursing. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T5#GNS324_U5_T5_h5)

question: What exactly is a nerve pathway?

options.A: An open space where hormones travel through the bloodstream
options.B: A blood vessel supplying oxygen directly to the brain cells
options.C: The protective fatty covering surrounding peripheral nerve fibers
options.D: The specific route electrical and chemical impulses travel through the nervous system

explanation: Think of a nerve pathway like a designated highway for your body's electrical signals, guiding messages smoothly from where they start to where they need to go! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT something food safety regulations normally check for?

options.A: Physical objects like metal shards or stones
options.B: Dangerous levels of chemical pesticide residues
options.C: Political views of the food manufacturing company owners
options.D: Harmful germs causing foodborne illnesses

explanation: Food safety is strictly about biological, chemical, and physical hazards—not who owns the company or what they believe! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h5)

question: A patient comes in with lower belly pain and a history of pelvic infections. Which tube-related complication should a nurse watch for closely?

options.A: Cervical dilation
options.B: Ovarian hyperstimulation
options.C: Ectopic pregnancy
options.D: Vaginal atrophy

explanation: Brilliant! Scarred fallopian tubes can trap a fertilized egg, leading to an ectopic pregnancy outside the uterus. Always keep an eye out for this! [learn more](GNS121_U5_T3#GNS121_U5_T3_h7)

question: What is a core responsibility of a community health nurse working with nurseries?

options.A: Managing the financial profits and tax returns of the facility
options.B: Replacing the parents as the primary legal guardian
options.C: Purchasing all commercial toys and playground equipment
options.D: Conducting health appraisals and checking immunization records

explanation: Community health nurses focus on health promotion, disease prevention, and monitoring vaccination compliance in childcare settings. [learn more](GNS225_U4_T8#GNS225_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is the absolute golden rule of diet therapy for a patient diagnosed with celiac disease?

options.A: Complete avoidance of all dairy and lactose products
options.B: A temporary increase in high-fiber whole grains
options.C: Lifelong strict elimination of dietary gluten
options.D: A high-sodium diet to prevent dehydration

explanation: Celiac disease triggers an immune reaction against gluten that damages the gut. Cutting out gluten completely is the only way the intestines can heal and stay healthy. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T008#GNS227_U7_T008_h5)

question: What does a sustainable elimination strategy primarily depend upon for long-term success?

options.A: Keeping all intervention data strictly secret from the public
options.B: Relying entirely on short-term foreign donor funding
options.C: Embedding prevention into national policies and health training
options.D: Punishing communities rather than engaging in dialogue

explanation: Sustainability means the work continues routinely through local systems, education, and government policy without fading away. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T18#GNS312_U1_T18_h8)

question: What is the main goal of using an explanatory research design in nursing?

options.A: To develop entirely new medical instruments for surgery
options.B: To uncover cause-and-effect relationships between variables
options.C: To count the exact frequency of a disease in a population
options.D: To observe patient behavior without any intervention

explanation: You've got this! Explanatory research simply looks at the 'why' and 'how' behind events by connecting different factors together. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T13#GNS224_U1_T13_h1)

question: How does a vision statement differ from a mission statement?

options.A: A vision statement is created by junior staff, while a mission is written by the government
options.B: A vision statement looks forward to future aspirations, while a mission focuses on present purpose
options.C: A vision statement is kept secret from patients, while a mission is printed on posters
options.D: A vision statement deals strictly with daily nursing chores, while a mission covers finances

explanation: Visions describe a future desired state, whereas missions focus on what the organization is doing today. [learn more](GST321_U2_T3#GST321_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which of these is a key way your blood helps regulate your body?

options.A: Maintaining normal body temperature
options.B: Generating electrical impulses for the heart
options.C: Synthesizing new digestive enzymes
options.D: Producing red bone marrow stem cells

explanation: Well done! Blood acts like a personal heating system, picking up heat from active muscles and sharing it around the body to keep you at a steady, safe temperature. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h2)

question: How do hookworm larvae usually enter the human body?

options.A: Bites from infected mosquitoes
options.B: Drinking unboiled river water
options.C: Direct penetration through the skin
options.D: Inhalation of airborne dust particles

explanation: Hookworm larvae love hanging out in contaminated soil. When people walk barefoot, these tiny worms can actually burrow right through the skin. Good reason to wear sandals! [learn more](GST114_U6_T3#GST114_U6_T3_h3)

question: When doing a home nutrition check, besides looking at physical health, what is a key thing to inspect?

options.A: Prescribing vitamin supplements to the family
options.B: Inspecting available food in the pantry
options.C: Weighing the patient once every month
options.D: Ordering laboratory blood tests immediately

explanation: Spot on! Checking the pantry and fridge helps you see the actual food the patient can reach and eat at home. You've got this! [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h1)

question: In rehabilitation, what does 'empowerment' really mean for a patient?

options.A: Supporting patients and their families to make their own choices
options.B: Using expensive imported equipment for all daily exercises
options.C: Making the patient completely dependent on healthcare workers
options.D: Limiting how much a patient is involved in their care plan

explanation: Brilliant! Empowerment means walking alongside patients so they take charge of their own recovery journey instead of just waiting to be told what to do. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T5#GNS225_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why is high blood potassium treated urgently in a patient with acute renal failure?

options.A: To encourage the kidneys to immediately start producing concentrated urine
options.B: To prevent severe infection in the upper urinary tract
options.C: To prevent dangerous and life-threatening heart rhythm changes
options.D: To stop the sudden breakdown of muscle tissue throughout the body

explanation: Elevated potassium levels severely affect the electrical system of the heart, leading to fatal cardiac arrhythmias if left untreated. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is a standardized classification system so important for nurses in the hospital?

options.A: It prevents patients from developing hospital-acquired infections
options.B: It helps healthcare teams communicate infectious disease risks clearly
options.C: It automatically lowers the cost of laboratory testing
options.D: It replaces the need for standard hand hygiene practices

explanation: When doctors, nurses, and lab scientists all use the same naming system, everyone is on the same page about which bug is making the patient sick. Teamwork makes the dream work! [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h1)

question: During a gastric lavage, a patient suddenly turns cyanotic, coughs hard, and has a drop in oxygen saturation. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Ask the patient to take deep breaths through their nose
options.B: Stop the procedure immediately and suction the airway
options.C: Instill more wash fluid to clear out any remaining blockages
options.D: Remove the protective endotracheal tube right away

explanation: These signs point to fluid aspiration into the lungs, requiring an immediate halt to fluid instillation and clearing of the airway to restore breathing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h7)

question: Why might a nursing student take a beta-blocker like propranolol before giving a major class presentation?

options.A: To increase their energy levels and stage presence
options.B: To cure their underlying social phobia permanently
options.C: To prevent them from falling asleep during the performance
options.D: To control physical symptoms like a racing heart and tremors

explanation: Beta-blockers block adrenaline, keeping your hands steady and heart calm without making your mind foggy. A real lifesaver for stage fright! [learn more](GNS314_U2_T6#GNS314_U2_T6_h7)

question: In nursing tests and exams, what does 'validity' actually mean?

options.A: The test can be completed in under twenty minutes.
options.B: Multiple instructors will always give the exact same grade.
options.C: The test gives the exact same score every single time it is used.
options.D: The test actually measures what it is intended to measure.

explanation: A valid test is one that truly assesses the exact skill or knowledge it claims to test. No tricks—just straight to the point! [learn more](GST321_U9_T3#GST321_U9_T3_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common barrier to mental health referrals in Nigeria?

options.A: High cost of transportation and out-of-pocket treatment expenses
options.B: Poor communication and missing feedback letters between facilities
options.C: Stigma and initial reliance on traditional or spiritual healers
options.D: Immediate availability of fully equipped psychiatric units in every rural village

explanation: Spot the trick! Fully equipped psychiatric units in every rural village definitely do not exist, making this option the false statement—and thus the correct answer. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T4#GNS314_U4_T4_h6)

question: Which nursing action is an example of primary prevention?

options.A: Checking blood pressure at a community health fair
options.B: Teaching foot care to a patient with diabetes
options.C: Providing cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
options.D: Administering a routine measles vaccine to a child

explanation: Vaccines stop a disease from occurring in the first place, which is the definition of primary prevention. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T2#GNS225_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which imaging test is the gold standard for catching a bone infection early?

options.A: Routine superficial ultrasound
options.B: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry
options.C: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
options.D: Standard plain radiography (X-ray)

explanation: X-rays take a while to show bone changes, but an MRI can spot early bone marrow changes and swelling super fast! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T18#GNS222_U1_T18_h5)

question: Which vitamin is given urgently to prevent permanent brain damage in patients with severe alcoholism?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Riboflavin
options.C: Thiamine
options.D: Vitamin K

explanation: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is a lifesaver here! Chronic alcohol use can severely deplete it, leading to serious brain issues like Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Quick replacement is key. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T9#GNS215_U6_T9_h5)

question: How do incident reporting systems help a hospital protect itself legally?

options.A: By ensuring nurses never have to document clinical procedures again
options.B: By identifying clinical system failures early so corrective action can be taken
options.C: By transferring all blame directly to the state ministry of health
options.D: By automatically hiding medical errors from patient legal representatives

explanation: Incident reports catch safety gaps early so management can fix them before they turn into major lawsuits and patient harm. [learn more](GST321_U10_T6#GST321_U10_T6_h7)

question: Which waste product builds up in the blood to cause hepatic encephalopathy?

options.A: Glucose
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Ammonia
options.D: Sodium

explanation: A healthy liver turns nitrogen waste like ammonia into safe urea. When the liver fails, ammonia builds up and affects brain function, causing confusion. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h4)

question: What happens right away when a bone gets fractured?

options.A: Immediate hardening of a permanent bony callus
options.B: Rapid degradation of surrounding articular cartilage
options.C: Instant conversion of osteoblasts into osteoclasts
options.D: Formation of a blood clot or fracture hematoma

explanation: When a bone breaks, blood vessels tear, and blood pools around the area to form a protective clot (hematoma) to kick off healing. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h5)

question: A conscious, alert adult refuses a life-saving treatment based on personal beliefs. Which ethical principle guides you to respect their choice?

options.A: Veracity
options.B: Beneficence
options.C: Justice
options.D: Autonomy

explanation: Well done! Autonomy means a competent patient has the right to decide what happens to their own body, even if we disagree with their choice. [learn more](GNS315_U1_T4#GNS315_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the main reason for having a patient keep a bladder diary?

options.A: To record fluid intake, leakage episodes, and voiding patterns
options.B: To list all daily medications and food allergies
options.C: To track blood pressure changes throughout the day
options.D: To measure daily weight fluctuations and calorie consumption

explanation: A bladder diary gives you a clear, real-life picture of when the patient drinks, when they leak, and how often they go. Super helpful for planning care! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: How does assertive behavior differ from aggressive behavior?

options.A: Assertiveness requires shouting to be heard clearly
options.B: Aggression is used exclusively by senior nursing staff
options.C: Assertiveness attacks the issue rather than the person
options.D: Aggression always leads to better patient outcomes

explanation: While aggression targets and belittles individuals, assertiveness keeps the focus firmly on solving the professional problem. [learn more](GST321_U7_T5#GST321_U7_T5_h1)

question: In the DESC communication script, what does the letter 'D' stand for?

options.A: Disregard the other person's emotions
options.B: Defend your personal clinical choices
options.C: Describe the specific behavior objectively
options.D: Demand immediate compliance from staff

explanation: Always start by stating the facts of what you saw, without throwing blame or making personal attacks. [learn more](GST321_U5_T4#GST321_U5_T4_h7)

question: About what percentage of total waste generated in a hospital is typically non-hazardous?

options.A: Zero percent
options.B: 75 to 90 percent
options.C: 10 to 25 percent
options.D: 40 to 50 percent

explanation: That's right! The vast majority of hospital refuse is actually general domestic-type waste that doesn't pose biological hazards. Keep it up! [learn more](GST114_U6_T5#GST114_U6_T5_h2)

question: How does endometriosis most commonly lead to infertility in women?

options.A: By causing pelvic adhesions and scarring that block the fallopian tubes
options.B: By lowering body temperature so much that embryos cannot implant
options.C: By destroying the pituitary gland and stopping all hormone production
options.D: By making the cervical mucus permanently hostile to male sperm cells

explanation: Spot on! Endometrial patches outside the womb cause ongoing inflammation and scar tissue, which can twist or block the tubes and ovaries. Keep crushing these questions! [learn more](GNS312_U1_T21#GNS312_U1_T21_h3)

question: A private hospital hires someone to work as a nurse without checking their credentials, and the person ends up harming a patient. What type of hospital liability applies here?

options.A: Strict criminal liability
options.B: Corporate negligence
options.C: Immunity from prosecution
options.D: Vicarious liability only

explanation: Failing to check qualifications is a direct failure by the institution itself. That is a textbook example of corporate negligence! [learn more](GST321_U10_T4#GST321_U10_T4_h6)

question: What is the main goal of public health agencies, as opposed to a regular hospital ward?

options.A: Managing health at a population level
options.B: Training medical doctors exclusively
options.C: Manufacturing pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: Providing surgical operations only

explanation: You've got this! While hospital wards focus on one sick patient at a time, public health agencies look at the big picture—keeping whole communities healthy and preventing disease. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T6#GNS112_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do many patients with severe, long-term lung disease experience noticeable weight loss and muscle wasting?

options.A: The physical effort of breathing uses up enormous amounts of energy
options.B: Their digestive tracts stop absorbing nutrients completely
options.C: They deliberately avoid eating to prevent shortness of breath
options.D: Liver damage prevents them from storing body fat

explanation: Think about how hard it is to run a race—now imagine working that hard just to breathe all day! That heavy effort burns massive amounts of energy and leads to weight loss. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h7)

question: What actually happens in the brain during a seizure?

options.A: A sudden, uncontrolled burst of electrical activity in the brain
options.B: A permanent loss of brain tissue caused by low oxygen
options.C: A complete cessation of all brainwave activity
options.D: A localized infection of the outer meninges

explanation: Think of a seizure like an electrical power surge in the brain. Brain cells suddenly fire signals all at once, which temporarily overloads the system and affects how a person moves, feels, or acts. You've got this! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T3#GNS223_U6_T3_h1)

question: What misconception do people sometimes hold about money spent on health care?

options.A: They think it only benefits retired politicians
options.B: They view it as a waste rather than a productive investment
options.C: They assume it is managed entirely by foreign countries
options.D: They believe it always causes inflation in food prices

explanation: Many budget planners incorrectly see health as a cost center rather than recognizing that a healthy population drives economic growth. [learn more](GST322_U5_T2#GST322_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why do researchers need to narrow down a massive topic like 'hospital stress'?

options.A: Broad topics are too massive and vague to study effectively all at once
options.B: Patients refuse to talk about general topics
options.C: Narrowing a topic increases the financial cost of the study
options.D: Broad topics are illegal to research in clinical settings

explanation: If your topic is as big as the ocean, you'll drown in data! Narrowing it down gives you a specific pool you can easily swim across. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T2#GNS217_U3_T2_h7)

question: Which glands add fluid to semen as it travels along the reproductive tract?

options.A: Sweat glands and sebaceous glands
options.B: Thyroid gland and pituitary gland
options.C: Seminal vesicles and prostate gland
options.D: Adrenal glands and pancreas

explanation: Great job! These helpful glands mix in fluids that feed the sperm and protect them from the acidic environment of the vagina. [learn more](GNS121_U4_T5#GNS121_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why should a researcher talk openly about the limitations of their study?

options.A: Delete the entire section if unexpected errors occurred
options.B: Pretend the study was completely flawless to impress readers
options.C: Acknowledge study flaws openly to show scientific integrity
options.D: Blame the research participants for making mistakes

explanation: No study is 100% perfect! Being honest about your weak spots actually builds trust and shows you really know your stuff. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T3#GNS224_U3_T3_h6)
